statement: In adults with alcohol dependence treated as outpatients in double-blind trials, mostly after detoxification and with counselling or another psychosocial treatment in both groups, naltrexone tablets at the dose used in most trials compared with placebo reduced return to heavy drinking (in most trials 5 or more drinks in a day for men, 4 or more for women) during 12 to 52 weeks of treatment: across 19 trials pooled in a review for the US Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality, 728 of 1,593 people on naltrexone (46 in 100) and 698 of 1,282 on placebo (54 in 100) returned to heavy drinking (crude totals, editors' arithmetic), a pooled difference of 9 in 100 (risk difference −0.09, 95% CI −0.13 to −0.04; 12 people treated for one to benefit) (Jonas et al., 2014; funded by the agency; no conflicts declared). Its 2023 update found a risk ratio of 0.81 (0.72 to 0.90; 23 trials, 3,170 people), and a Cochrane review of naltrexone in any form, mostly the same tablets, 0.83 (0.76 to 0.90; 28 trials, 4,433 people) (McPheeters et al., 2023; Rösner et al., 2010). The effect on staying off alcohol completely was small or unclear: risk difference −0.05 (−0.10 to −0.002) in 2014, risk ratio 0.93 (0.87 to 0.99) in 2023 and 0.96 (0.92 to 1.00) in the Cochrane review. People on naltrexone drank on about 5 fewer days in every 100 (−5.1 percentage points, −7.16 to −3.04) and drank heavily on about 4 fewer (−4.3, −7.60 to −0.91). Nausea (risk ratio 1.73, 1.51 to 1.98), dizziness (1.99, 1.47 to 2.69) and vomiting (1.53, 1.23 to 1.91) were more common, about 1 more person in 48 stopped a trial because of side effects (number needed to harm 48, 30 to 112), and serious adverse events were not more frequent (risk difference −0.02, −0.05 to 0.00; 9 trials). A higher oral dose and a long-acting injection were each tested in only 2 or 3 trials, without a clear effect on return to heavy drinking. Head to head, naltrexone and acamprosate did not differ (return to heavy drinking risk ratio 1.02, 0.93 to 1.11; 4 trials, more than half of the people in one US trial). Evidence on deaths, injuries and quality of life is insufficient. The three reviews share most of their trials and are one body of evidence, not three. Most participants were White men in their 40s with moderate to severe dependence who had stopped drinking before starting, and effects in people still drinking, with mild disorder or without counselling are uncertain. Certainty: moderate. Status: replicated.
plain: In trials lasting 3 months to a year, people with alcohol dependence who took naltrexone tablets went back to heavy drinking less often than people on dummy pills: about 46 in 100 against 54 in 100. Naltrexone helped less, if at all, with stopping drinking completely. People on it drank on about 5 fewer days in every 100. Feeling sick, dizziness and vomiting were more common, and about 1 more person in 48 stopped because of side effects. Naltrexone and acamprosate did about the same when compared directly. Most people in the trials were middle-aged men who had already stopped drinking and also had counselling.
population: Adults with alcohol dependence (DSM-III-R, DSM-IV or ICD-10) treated as outpatients in double-blind randomized trials of 12 to 52 weeks (4 weeks or more in the Cochrane review), mostly after detoxification or a few days without alcohol and with a psychosocial co-intervention in both groups; mostly White men in their 40s, more trials in the US than elsewhere
exposure: Naltrexone tablets at the dose used in most trials (analysed apart from a higher oral dose and from the long-acting injection in the AHRQ reviews; any form, mostly the same tablets, in the Cochrane review)
comparator: Placebo with the same co-intervention; acamprosate in head-to-head trials
outcome: Return to heavy drinking and to any drinking during treatment; percentage of drinking days and of heavy drinking days; side effects, stopping a trial because of them, and serious adverse events; deaths and other health outcomes
magnitude: Jonas et al. 2014 (oral naltrexone, main dose group, against placebo): return to heavy drinking RD −0.09 (95% CI −0.13 to −0.04), 19 trials, 2875 participants, I² 43.7%, NNT 12 (8 to 26), moderate strength of evidence; crude totals 728/1593 (45.7%) against 698/1282 (54.4%) (editors' arithmetic from Figure 3); return to any drinking RD −0.05 (−0.10 to −0.002), 16 trials, 2347, NNT 20 (11 to 500); percentage of drinking days WMD −5.4 (−7.5 to −3.2); heavy drinking days −4.1 (−7.6 to −0.61); withdrawal from trials because of adverse events NNH 48 (30 to 112), 17 trials, 2743. McPheeters et al. 2023: return to heavy drinking RR 0.81 (0.72 to 0.90), 23 trials, 3170, moderate; return to any drinking 0.93 (0.87 to 0.99), 16 trials, 2347, moderate; percentage of drinking days −5.1 (−7.16 to −3.04), 15 trials; heavy drinking days −4.3 (−7.60 to −0.91), 7 trials; any dose, return to heavy drinking 0.86 (0.80 to 0.93), 27 trials, 4645; higher oral dose 0.93 (0.84 to 1.01), 2 trials, and injection 1.00 (0.82 to 1.21), 2 trials, both low; nausea RR 1.73 (1.51 to 1.98), dizziness 1.99 (1.47 to 2.69), vomiting 1.53 (1.23 to 1.91); acamprosate against naltrexone, return to any drinking 1.03 (0.96 to 1.10), 3 trials, 800, return to heavy drinking 1.02 (0.93 to 1.11), 4 trials, 1141; deaths 1 against 2 (6 trials, 1738), insufficient. Rösner et al. 2010 (Cochrane): return to heavy drinking RR 0.83 (0.76 to 0.90), 28 trials, 4433, NNTB 9.09 (6.66 to 14.28); return to any drinking 0.96 (0.92 to 1.00), 27 trials, 4693 (fixed effect 0.95, 0.92 to 0.98); drinking days MD −3.89 (−5.75 to −2.04); nausea RD 0.10 (0.07 to 0.13); serious adverse events RD −0.02 (−0.05 to 0.00), 9 trials; drop-out because of adverse events RR 1.60 (1.15 to 2.23), 22 trials.

evidence.extracted: Oral naltrexone (the review's main dose group) against placebo, trials at low or medium risk of bias: return to heavy drinking RD −0.09 (95% CI −0.13 to −0.04), 19 trials, n = 2875, I² 43.7%, NNT 12 (8 to 26), moderate strength of evidence; return to any drinking RD −0.05 (−0.10 to −0.002), 16 trials, n = 2347, NNT 20 (11 to 500), moderate; percentage of drinking days WMD −5.4 (−7.5 to −3.2), 15 trials, n = 1992; percentage of heavy drinking days −4.1 (−7.6 to −0.61), 6 trials, n = 521; drinks per drinking day −0.49 (−0.92 to −0.06), 9 trials, low strength. RDs are absolute differences in the proportion of participants. Editors' arithmetic from the event counts of the 19 trials in Figure 3: 728 of 1593 (45.7%) on naltrexone and 698 of 1282 (54.4%) on placebo returned to heavy drinking (crude totals, not the random-effects estimate).

123 studies were included (one a prospective cohort study, the rest RCTs; 22 803 participants); naltrexone was studied in 53 (n = 9140), with 44 placebo-controlled trials. Treatment lasted 12 to 52 weeks and mean age was usually in the 40s; participants met criteria for alcohol dependence in the vast majority of trials and were mostly enrolled after detoxification or at least 3 days of abstinence. Most studies included psychosocial co-interventions, so effect sizes reflect the added benefit of medication beyond psychosocial interventions and placebo.

Withdrawal from trials because of adverse events was more frequent with naltrexone than with placebo, NNH 48 (95% CI 30 to 112; 17 trials, n = 2743); those on naltrexone also had a higher risk of dizziness (NNH 16), nausea (NNH 9) and vomiting (NNH 24).

evidence.locator: Discussion › Applicability of Findings, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 1896); Discussion › Limitations, 2nd paragraph (p. 1897)
evidence.extracted: Most participants met DSM-III or DSM-IV criteria for alcohol dependence, likely moderate to severe disorder in DSM-5 terms, so applicability to mild disorder is uncertain; mean age was generally in the 40s and there was no evidence on whether benefit differs by age or other characteristics. Of 44 placebo-controlled naltrexone trials, 27 were in the US and 8 in Europe. Few studies were rated at low risk of bias (8 of 123; 4 of 53 naltrexone studies); most were medium risk because of incomplete reporting of sequence generation, allocation concealment, fidelity, adherence or outcome-assessor masking.

risk_of_bias.note: Few trials were at low risk of bias: 4 of 53 naltrexone studies in Jonas et al.; allocation concealment adequate in 3 of 50 and missing binary data adequately handled in 11 of 40 in the Cochrane review; drinking was self-reported. The reviews' own AMSTAR 2 ratings are critically low (Jonas; McPheeters) and low (Rösner), mainly for documentation.

inconsistency.note: Moderate heterogeneity (I² 43.7% in 2014, 58.7% in 2023) with most trials on the same side; the Cochrane review's approximate prediction interval (RR 0.61 to 1.12, editors' calculation on its study card) shows that single trials may find no effect, which the statement allows for.

indirectness.note: Worded for the trial populations (detoxified, mostly treatment-seeking adults with moderate to severe dependence, with counselling); the uncertainty outside them is stated.

imprecision.note: Thousands of participants and intervals that exclude no effect for return to heavy drinking.

publication_bias.note: Funnel plots and Begg's or Egger's tests showed no clear asymmetry in two reviews, and industry and non-profit trials gave similar estimates; the 2023 review did not assess publication bias.

grade.reasoning: Randomized trials start high; rated down one level for risk of bias, giving moderate, as both AHRQ reviews graded return to heavy drinking. 'Reduces' applies to return to heavy drinking; the effect on any drinking is small and depends on the review and model (significant in 2014 and 2023, not in the Cochrane random-effects model), and the claim says so. Overlap: the 2023 review updates the 2014 one (81 of its 118 trials carried over), the Cochrane review covers largely the same trials to January 2010, and COMBINE is in all three, so they are counted as one body of evidence. Status replicated: that body holds many independent trials pointing the same way. The higher oral dose and the injection are named only as tested in 2 or 3 trials; no doses are given.
